en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Buddha, concerning the Question on Inference.

8. The Question on the Immoral One “Venerable Nāgasena, what is the distinction between a layman who is immoral and a monk who is immoral? What is the difference between them? Do both go to the same destination, and does the result for both of them become exactly the same? Or is there some difference?
“Great King, there are these ten qualities by which a monk who is immoral excels and surpasses a layman who is immoral; and for ten reasons, he purifies the offering more effectively.”
What are the ten qualities by which a monk of immoral conduct excels and surpasses a householder of immoral conduct?

Here, Great King, a monk of immoral conduct possesses reverence for the Buddha, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, and reverence for his fellow practitioners; he exerts himself in recitation and interrogation, and is devoted to hearing the teachings.
There is, Great King, the immoral one who, though of broken virtue, enters an assembly and maintains a proper deportment;
out of fear of reproach, he guards his bodily and verbal conduct, and his mind is directed toward exertion; he has entered the state of a monk’s renunciation.
Even so, Great King, the immoral ascetic practices evil deeds while concealing them.
Just as, Great King, a woman with a husband might commit an evil act in secret while remaining hidden;
even so, Great King, a corrupt ascetic, though acting, commits evil in concealment.
These, Great King, are the ten qualities by which a corrupt ascetic excels and surpasses a corrupt householder.
By what ten reasons does one further purify the offering?
One purifies the offering by wearing the armor of blamelessness; one purifies the offering by wearing the robes, bowl, and marks of the sages and recluses;
one purifies the offering by having entered into the discipline of the Saṅgha; and one purifies the offering by having gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
One purifies the offering by dwelling in a place for striving and a dwelling for exertion; one purifies the offering by seeking out those who uphold the Conqueror’s teaching;
one purifies the offering by the teaching of the sublime Dhamma; one purifies the offering by taking refuge in the lamp of the Dhamma as one’s final goal;
one purifies the offering by holding the exclusive view that “the Buddha is supreme”; and one purifies the offering by undertaking the observance day (uposatha).
He purifies the offering.
It is by these ten reasons, Great King, that one purifies an offering further.
For even a corrupt ascetic of immoral conduct, Great King, though he has utterly failed, purifies the offering of the donors.
Just as water, O Great King, removes even a great deal of mire, mud, dust, and filth;
even so, O Great King, does a monk who is ill-behaved and of bad character purify the offering of those who give.
Or again, O Great King, just as hot water, though slightly heated, extinguishes a great, blazing mass of fire.
In the same way, Great King, even a corrupt ascetic who has utterly failed purifies the offering of those who give.
Or again, Great King, just as food, even if tasteless, removes the weakness of hunger;
in the same way, Great King, even a corrupt ascetic who has utterly failed purifies the offering of those who give.
This was spoken, Great King, by the Tathāgata, the God beyond Gods, in the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta*, the exposition on offerings, within the *Majjhima Nikāya*:
“When one who is virtuous gives a gift to those who are immoral,
having acquired it righteously and with a mind full of serene confidence;”
“Having full confidence in the sublime fruit of action, that offering is purified by the giver.

“It is wonderful, venerable Nāgasena! It is marvelous, venerable Nāgasena! We have asked you so many questions, and you, by explaining them through similes and reasons, have made them as sweet as the Deathless to hear.”
“Just as, venerable sir, a cook or a cook’s apprentice, having obtained a certain amount of meat, prepares it with various ingredients and makes it a delicacy for a king;
even so, venerable Nāgasena, we asked you only so much of a question, yet you have elucidated it with similes and reasons, making it reach our ears sweet as the Deathless.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, “The Question on Immorality.”
